stances.claim: The four Cs (careful, calculated, calibrated, courteous) and the deliberate ambiguity across Duterte, Roque, Locsin, and Lorenzana are not contradiction but the legitimate practice of executive-privileged foreign policy -- short-term tactical confusion serving long-term strategy.
stances.rhetorical_move: executive-privilege framing to explain apparent administration cacophony

stances.claim: Locsin's outburst was 'borne of pique' over 78 inadequately answered diplomatic protests -- emotionally understandable, but not the canonical mode of diplomacy; the next-day apology and Roque's chain-of-command reminder restored the protocol that only the President may use cuss words.

What the Philippines is fighting for is UNCLOS as applied by the July 12, 2016 AA on maritime entitlements -- but arbitral awards, including the AA, are NOT parts of international law and are NOT precedents for future arbitrations; they are binding only on the parties thereto.
stances.rhetorical_move: candid-doctrinal-limit disclosure (CJ flagging the awkward truth about awards)
stances.confidence: asserted with self-disclosure ('I would be the last person to devalue arbitrations')

stances.claim: China refuses to recognize the AA on the doctrinal ground that WPS issues involve LAND sovereignty, which only the ICJ has jurisdiction over -- a position that, however inconvenient, has technical force.

The right path is to accept China's challenge and take the dispute to the ICJ -- ICJ decisions have precedent value, are parts of international law, and are invariably implemented by the UN; the great powers (including the US, whose national chairs the ICJ) all have sitting members, so the playing field is not skewed.
stances.rhetorical_move: ICJ-pathway recommendation echoing the April 25 column

notable_anecdotes: The four-C catalog -- Roque's three Cs (Careful, Calculated, Calibrated) plus Duterte's added Courteous -- laid out as the administration's alliterative WPS doctrine, then deployed as the title and structuring device of the column.

Duterte's recall of his Xi conversation -- 'Filipinos are hungry, and you are not oblivious to that fact. So, kindly just allow our fishermen to fish in peace' -- the most domesticated, almost-personal idiom for sovereign-rights diplomacy.

Locsin's GET-THE-FUCK-OUT tweet and his ugly-oaf-vs-handsome-guy simile -- used not just for color but as the moment that triggered Roque's invocation of the chain-of-command speech protocol ('only the President... may use cuss words').

CJ's self-disclosure of his role as chair of the Philippine National Group in the PCA -- along with the named roster of the only other Filipino PCA members (Pangalangan, Puno, Vitug) -- as the credentials anchoring his candid concession that arbitral awards are not parts of international law.
'No permanent friends or permanent enemies, only permanent national interests' -- quoted as the underlying truth of all foreign-policy ambiguity.
The teaser line 'Is the AA a mere scrap of paper? The answer deserves a future column' -- leaving the doctrinal question to next week.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban catalogues the four 'Cs' shaping the administration's West Philippine Sea posture -- spokesperson Harry Roque's three (careful, calculated, calibrated) plus President Duterte's added 'courteous' from his May 3 televised address ('China remains to be our benefactor'). He contrasts these with Foreign Secretary Teddy Locsin's blunt tweet 'GET THE FUCK OUT' addressed to China -- likening Beijing to 'an ugly oaf forcing your attentions on a handsome guy' -- and the next-day apology after Roque's reminder that only the President may use cuss words in diplomacy. Locsin's pique, CJ suggests, came from 78 inadequately answered diplomatic protests since 2016 and the May 3 accusation that Chinese coast-guard vessels were 'shadowing, blocking, [conducting] dangerous maneuvers, and radio challenges' against the PCG. Defense Secretary Delfin Lorenzana was more calibrated ('We will defend what is rightfully ours without going to war') while dispatching the Navy's gray vessels to patrol the WPS, and the PCG shooed away seven Chinese militia vessels. CJ explains that under Senate v. Ermita (2006), the President and Cabinet enjoy executive privilege over state secrets -- making ambiguity sometimes the deliberate cover for long-term strategy: 'No permanent friends or permanent enemies, only permanent national interests.' What the four Cs are fighting for is UNCLOS as applied by the July 12, 2016 Arbitral Award -- but, candidly conceding the doctrinal reality (he chairs the Philippine National Group in the Permanent Court of Arbitration), CJ notes that arbitral awards are not parts of international law and not precedents for future arbitrations; they are binding only on the parties. China's refusal to recognize the AA -- on the ground that WPS issues involve LAND sovereignty falling only under ICJ jurisdiction -- has technical force. He reiterates his April 25 plea: accept China's challenge and let the ICJ decide. ICJ decisions are international law, have precedent value, and are invariably implemented by the UN -- and the great powers (US, Japan, France, Germany) all have sitting ICJ members, with the ICJ president himself an American.
